sections.title: From steady DC to the restless sine wave

board_events.text: DC pushes one way. AC never stops changing its mind.

board_events.caption: Steady DC line against an alternating sine wave

board_events.latex: i = i_m \sin \omega t, \qquad v = v_m \sin \omega t

board_events.text: i_m is the peak, or amplitude: the largest value the current ever reaches.

board_events.caption: Amplitude and period on one sine cycle

board_events.text: Indian mains: f = 50 Hz, so 50 complete back-and-forth cycles every second.
Why AC? Transformers step AC up and down almost losslessly. DC cannot do that simply.
High transmission voltage means tiny current, and the wasted heat collapses.

segments.text: <curious> Let us start with the thing that separates this whole chapter from everything you have done before. A direct current, D C, flows steadily in one direction. Think of the current from a cell: it always pushes the same way, and it never changes its mind.

Alternating current is restless. Look at the picture. The green line is D C, flat and dependable. The blue curve is A C, and watch what it does: it grows, it falls back to zero, it reverses direction completely, and then it repeats the whole story. Almost every electron moving in the world right now is doing exactly this.

And the shape it takes is the sine wave. The instantaneous current is i equals i m sine omega t, and the instantaneous voltage is v equals v m sine omega t. Same shape, same rhythm, just different quantities riding on it.

That subscript m matters. i m is the peak, also called the amplitude. It is the largest value the current reaches, at the very top of each hump. Notice it is an instantaneous maximum, touched only for an instant twice per cycle, not a value the current holds.

Omega is the angular frequency, and it is two pi f, which is also two pi divided by the time period T. So omega is just frequency wearing radian clothing. If you know any one of omega, f, or T, this single relation hands you the other two.

Here is the anatomy of one cycle. The amplitude i m is the height from the axis to the crest. The period T is the horizontal width of one complete story: up, down through zero, into the negative, and back. Everything else in this chapter is measured against these two numbers.

For Indian mains, the frequency is fifty hertz. So the period is one over fifty, which is nought point nought two seconds, and omega is two pi times fifty, which is one hundred pi, roughly three hundred fourteen radians per second. Memorise this trio; it appears in question after question.

Now the obvious question. Why does the world tolerate this restless current instead of clean, steady D C? One reason towers over all the others. A C voltage can be stepped up and down almost losslessly by a transformer. D C cannot do this simply.

And that matters because the heat wasted in a transmission line goes as current squared times resistance. Push the voltage up, and for the same delivered power the current must come down, so the waste collapses. A C is also easier to generate. The price we pay is purely conceptual, and that price is the rest of this section.

<curious> चलिए उस चीज़ से शुरू करते हैं जो इस पूरे chapter को अलग बनाती है। Direct current, यानी D C, steadily एक ही direction में flow करता है। Cell का current सोचिए: वो हमेशा एक ही तरफ push करता है, कभी अपना मन नहीं बदलता।

Alternating current restless है। Picture देखिए। हरी line D C है, flat और dependable। नीली curve A C है, और देखिए ये क्या करती है: बढ़ती है, वापस zero पर गिरती है, पूरी तरह direction reverse करती है, और फिर यही कहानी दोहराती है। दुनिया में अभी जो electrons move कर रहे हैं, लगभग सब यही कर रहे हैं।
और जो shape ये लेता है वो है sine wave। Instantaneous current है i equals i m sine omega t, और instantaneous voltage है v equals v m sine omega t। वही shape, वही rhythm, बस quantity अलग है।

वो subscript m important है। i m है peak, जिसे amplitude भी कहते हैं। ये current की सबसे बड़ी value है, हर hump के बिल्कुल top पर। ध्यान दीजिए ये instantaneous maximum है, per cycle सिर्फ़ दो बार एक पल के लिए छुआ जाता है, कोई ऐसी value नहीं जो current hold करके रखे।

Omega है angular frequency, और ये है two pi f, जो two pi divided by time period T भी है। तो omega बस frequency है radian कपड़ों में। अगर omega, f, या T में से कोई एक पता है, तो यही एक relation बाकी दोनों दे देता है।

ये रही एक cycle की anatomy। Amplitude i m axis से crest तक की height है। Period T एक पूरी कहानी की horizontal width है: ऊपर, zero से नीचे, negative में, और वापस। इस chapter में बाकी सब कुछ इन्हीं दो numbers के against मापा जाता है।

Indian mains के लिए frequency fifty hertz है। तो period one over fifty यानी nought point nought two second, और omega two pi times fifty यानी one hundred pi, लगभग three hundred fourteen radian per second। ये तिकड़ी याद कर लीजिए; question दर question आती है।

अब obvious सवाल। दुनिया साफ़-सुथरे steady D C की जगह इस restless current को क्यों बर्दाश्त करती है? एक वजह बाकी सब पर भारी है। A C voltage को transformer से almost losslessly step up और step down किया जा सकता है। D C ये आसानी से नहीं कर सकता।

और ये इसलिए matter करता है क्योंकि transmission line में बर्बाद होने वाली heat current squared times resistance जाती है। Voltage ऊपर कीजिए, तो same delivered power के लिए current नीचे आना ही पड़ेगा, और waste गिर जाता है। A C generate करना भी आसान है। जो कीमत हम चुकाते हैं वो purely conceptual है, और वही कीमत इस section का बाकी हिस्सा है।

sections.title: Why the average fails and RMS is born

board_events.text: How strong is the mains? The average will not answer.
Over a full cycle AC spends as much time positive as negative, so its average is exactly zero.
Yet it lights a bulb. So zero average cannot mean zero effect.

board_events.caption: Current can be negative, but current squared never is

board_events.text: A resistor does not care which way current flows. Heating depends on i squared, always positive.
The honest question: what steady DC would heat the same resistor equally?

board_events.caption: AC and its DC-equivalent produce identical heating

board_events.text: RMS is the effective or DC-equivalent value. Every AC meter reads it; every appliance is rated in it.

segments.text: Suppose someone points at a wall socket and asks you a simple question: how strong is that? You would like to answer with a single number. The trouble is that the current there is different at every instant, so which instant do you quote?

Your first instinct is the average. That instinct fails, and it fails completely. Over one full cycle, an alternating current spends exactly as much time positive as it does negative, and those two halves cancel perfectly. The average over a full cycle is not small. It is exactly zero.

But an exactly zero average would mean the mains does nothing at all, and that is obviously false. It lights bulbs, it runs motors, it delivers real energy every second. So the honest conclusion is that the average is asking the wrong question.

Here is the right question, and the picture shows why. On top is the current, negative for half of every cycle. Underneath is the current squared, and notice it never dips below the axis at all. Squaring destroys the sign.

That is not a mathematical trick, it is physics. A resistor does not care which direction the charge flows through it. It heats up either way, because the heating rate depends on i squared, and i squared is always positive. The negative half of the cycle heats the resistor just as enthusiastically as the positive half.

So we change the question. Instead of asking how big the current is on average, we ask: what steady D C current, flowing through this same resistor, would produce exactly the same heating? That number is a real, honest, single answer.

<excited> And that is exactly what the picture shows. On the left, an A C source of peak i m driving a resistor R. On the right, a D C source driving an identical resistor. Choose the D C current correctly and the two resistors get equally hot. They are thermally indistinguishable.

That equivalent value is the root mean square current, and its name is a literal set of instructions read backwards. Square the current, take the mean of that square over a cycle, then take the square root. R M S: root, of the mean, of the square.

So R M S is the effective value, or the D C-equivalent value. This is what every A C meter on the planet reads, and what every appliance is rated for. When your board says two hundred twenty volts, it is quoting R M S, and now you know precisely what that promise means: it heats like two hundred twenty volts of steady D C would.

मान लीजिए कोई wall socket की तरफ़ इशारा करके एक simple सवाल पूछता है: ये कितना strong है? आप एक single number से जवाब देना चाहेंगे। मुश्किल ये है कि वहाँ current हर instant पर अलग है, तो कौन सा instant quote करें?

पहली instinct होती है average। ये instinct fail होती है, और पूरी तरह fail होती है। एक full cycle में alternating current उतना ही समय positive रहता है जितना negative, और दोनों halves perfectly cancel हो जाते हैं। Full cycle का average छोटा नहीं है। वो exactly zero है।

लेकिन exactly zero average का मतलब होता कि mains कुछ करता ही नहीं, और ये obviously ग़लत है। वो bulb जलाता है, motor चलाता है, हर second real energy देता है। तो ईमानदार conclusion यही है कि average ग़लत सवाल पूछ रहा है।
ये रहा सही सवाल, और picture दिखाती है क्यों। ऊपर current है, हर cycle के आधे हिस्से में negative। नीचे current squared है, और देखिए ये axis के नीचे कभी जाता ही नहीं। Squaring sign को मिटा देती है।

ये कोई mathematical trick नहीं, ये physics है। Resistor को परवाह नहीं कि charge किस direction में बह रहा है। वो दोनों तरह गरम होता है, क्योंकि heating rate i squared पर depend करता है, और i squared हमेशा positive है। Cycle का negative half resistor को उतने ही जोश से गरम करता है जितना positive half।

तो हम सवाल बदल देते हैं। ये पूछने की जगह कि current average में कितना बड़ा है, हम पूछते हैं: कौन सा steady D C current, इसी resistor से बहकर, exactly वही heating पैदा करेगा? ये number एक real, ईमानदार, single जवाब है।

<excited> और picture यही दिखाती है। बाईं तरफ़ peak i m वाला A C source एक resistor R चला रहा है। दाईं तरफ़ एक D C source वैसा ही resistor चला रहा है। D C current सही चुनिए और दोनों resistor बराबर गरम होंगे। वो thermally indistinguishable हैं।

वो equivalent value है root mean square current, और इसका नाम उल्टा पढ़ा गया instruction set है। Current को square कीजिए, cycle पर उस square का mean लीजिए, फिर square root लीजिए। R M S: root, of the mean, of the square।

तो R M S है effective value, या D C-equivalent value। दुनिया का हर A C meter यही पढ़ता है, और हर appliance इसी पर rated होता है। जब आपका board कहता है two hundred twenty volt, वो R M S quote कर रहा है, और अब आप जानते हैं उस वादे का exact मतलब: ये उतना गरम करता है जितना two hundred twenty volt का steady D C करता।

sections.title: The half-cycle mean, the phasor, and where the clean factors break

board_events.text: A second, weaker measure: the mean over the positive half only

board_events.caption: Half-cycle mean against the cancelling full cycle

board_events.text: Useful for charge delivered by a half-wave rectifier, where only one half survives.
The phasor: a rotating arrow whose shadow is the wave

board_events.caption: Rotating phasor and the sine it projects

board_events.text: Arrow length = amplitude. It spins anticlockwise at angular speed omega.
This is exactly the reference-circle picture of simple harmonic motion.
The clean factors 0.707 and 0.637 hold ONLY for a pure sinusoid. Square or triangular waves need the integral redone.
220 V mains always means the RMS value. Never the peak.

segments.text: R M S is the headline measure, but there is a second one, weaker but genuinely useful, and examiners like it precisely because students forget it. It is the mean value taken over only the positive half cycle.

The picture makes the logic visible. The shaded region is the area under one positive hump. Over the full cycle, the negative hump has exactly equal area with the opposite sign, so everything cancels and the full-cycle average is zero. Restrict yourself to the positive half alone and a real, non-zero number survives: nought point six three seven times the peak.

Where does that matter? Anywhere only one half of the wave gets through. A half-wave rectifier chops off the negative half, so the charge it delivers is governed by this half-cycle mean, not by the R M S. Always state which average you mean, because there are two of them and they differ.
Now the tool that makes the rest of this chapter possible, and it costs nothing to learn because you already know it from oscillations. It is called the phasor, and it is simply a rotating arrow.

Look at the left half of the picture. There is an arrow whose length equals the amplitude, spinning anticlockwise at angular speed omega. Now drop its tip straight onto the vertical axis. That shadow, that projection, is the instantaneous value at that moment. Let the arrow keep spinning and its shadow traces out the sine wave on the right, point by point.

So the arrow carries two pieces of information at once: how big the quantity is, in its length, and where in the cycle it currently sits, in its angle. That second piece is exactly what a bare number cannot carry, and it is what we will desperately need in the next subtopic.

<curious> And if this feels familiar, it should. This is precisely the reference circle you drew for simple harmonic motion. Same circle, same omega, same projection. The only change is that the rotating quantity is now a voltage or a current instead of a displacement. Physics reused the machinery.

One serious caution before we move on. Those clean factors, nought point seven zero seven for R M S and nought point six three seven for the half-cycle mean, are not universal constants. They come from integrating a sine. A square wave, a triangular wave, or a rectified wave gives different numbers, and you must redo the integral from scratch.

<whisper> And the single most examined line in this subtopic: two hundred twenty volt mains always means the R M S value. Never the peak. If a question hands you a rated voltage without the word peak attached, it is R M S, and the peak is root two times larger.
R M S headline measure है, लेकिन एक दूसरी भी है, कमज़ोर पर सचमुच useful, और examiners को यही पसंद है क्योंकि students इसे भूल जाते हैं। ये है सिर्फ़ positive half cycle पर लिया गया mean value।

Picture logic को visible बना देती है। Shaded region एक positive hump के नीचे का area है। Full cycle पर negative hump का area exactly बराबर है पर opposite sign के साथ, तो सब cancel हो जाता है और full-cycle average zero रहता है। खुद को सिर्फ़ positive half तक सीमित कीजिए और एक real non-zero number बचता है: nought point six three seven times peak।

ये कहाँ matter करता है? जहाँ भी wave का सिर्फ़ एक half गुज़र पाता है। Half-wave rectifier negative half काट देता है, तो जो charge वो deliver करता है वो इसी half-cycle mean से चलता है, R M S से नहीं। हमेशा बताइए कौन सा average, क्योंकि दो हैं और वो अलग हैं।
अब वो tool जो इस chapter का बाकी हिस्सा possible बनाता है, और सीखने में कुछ नहीं लगता क्योंकि आप इसे oscillations से पहले से जानते हैं। इसे phasor कहते हैं, और ये बस एक rotating arrow है।

Picture का बायाँ हिस्सा देखिए। एक arrow है जिसकी length amplitude के बराबर है, anticlockwise angular speed omega से घूमती हुई। अब उसकी tip को सीधे vertical axis पर गिराइए। वो shadow, वो projection, उस पल की instantaneous value है। Arrow को घूमने दीजिए और उसका shadow दाईं तरफ़ point by point sine wave बना देता है।

तो arrow एक साथ दो जानकारियाँ ढोती है: quantity कितनी बड़ी है, अपनी length में, और cycle में अभी कहाँ बैठी है, अपने angle में। दूसरी जानकारी ठीक वही है जो एक अकेला number नहीं ढो सकता, और अगले subtopic में हमें उसी की सख़्त ज़रूरत पड़ेगी।

<curious> और अगर ये जाना-पहचाना लग रहा है, तो लगना ही चाहिए। ये exactly वही reference circle है जो आपने simple harmonic motion में बनाया था। वही circle, वही omega, वही projection। फ़र्क़ सिर्फ़ इतना कि घूमने वाली quantity अब displacement की जगह voltage या current है। Physics ने machinery दोबारा इस्तेमाल कर ली।

आगे बढ़ने से पहले एक गंभीर चेतावनी। वो साफ़ factors, R M S के लिए nought point seven zero seven और half-cycle mean के लिए nought point six three seven, universal constants नहीं हैं। वो sine को integrate करने से आते हैं। Square wave, triangular wave, या rectified wave अलग numbers देती है, और integral दोबारा शुरू से करना पड़ेगा।

<whisper> और इस subtopic की सबसे ज़्यादा पूछी जाने वाली line: two hundred twenty volt mains का मतलब हमेशा R M S value है। Peak कभी नहीं। अगर question आपको rated voltage देता है और peak शब्द नहीं लिखा, तो वो R M S है, और peak root two गुना बड़ा है।

board_events.text: Mains, worth memorising: 220 V rms gives 311 V peak; 50 Hz gives T = 0.02 s and omega = 100 pi.
Units: i_m and I_rms in ampere; v_m and V_rms in volt; omega in radian per second; form and peak factors dimensionless.

segments.text: Here is the complete toolkit for this subtopic on one board. Everything else in these sections is either the derivation of one of these lines or a numerical that feeds them.

Start with the instantaneous values. The current is i m sine omega t and the voltage is v m sine omega t, with omega equal to two pi f, which also equals two pi over T. These three quantities, omega, f, and T, are interchangeable, so a question that gives you any one has effectively given you all three.

The R M S values. I r m s equals i m divided by root two, which is nought point seven zero seven times the peak, and the voltage relation is identical in form. Root two, not two. That single slip is the most common wrong answer in the entire subtopic, so let it register now.

The half-cycle mean. I average equals two i m over pi, which is nought point six three seven times the peak. Notice pi in the denominator, which is the fingerprint of an integration over a half sine, and we will see exactly that integration in two sections from now.

Two ratios that J E E Main likes to ask for by name. The form factor is R M S divided by half-cycle mean, which works out to pi over two root two, equal to one point one one. The peak factor is peak divided by R M S, which is simply root two, one point four one four. Both are pure numbers with no units.

And the reason R M S was invented in the first place: average power in a resistor. It equals I r m s squared times R, and equally V r m s times I r m s, and equally V r m s squared over R. Look at those three forms carefully. They are exactly the D C power formulas with R M S values substituted in. That is not a coincidence; it is the entire design goal.

<excited> Now burn this ladder into your memory, because it is a free error-check on every answer you will ever write here. The half-cycle mean sits lowest at nought point six three seven of the peak. R M S sits above it at nought point seven zero seven. The peak sits highest. Mean, then R M S, then peak, always in that order for a sinusoid.

The mains numbers are worth memorising outright rather than deriving under exam pressure. Two hundred twenty volt R M S means a peak of two hundred twenty root two, which is about three hundred eleven volts. Fifty hertz means the period is nought point nought two seconds and omega is one hundred pi, roughly three hundred fourteen radians per second.

Finally the units, because dimensional slips cost easy marks. Peak and R M S currents are both in ampere, peak and R M S voltages both in volt, since R M S does not change what kind of quantity something is. Omega is radians per second. Form factor and peak factor are ratios of like quantities, so they are dimensionless.
ये रहा इस subtopic का पूरा toolkit एक board पर। इन sections में बाकी सब या तो इनमें से किसी line का derivation है या कोई numerical जो इन्हें feed करता है।

Instantaneous values से शुरू। Current है i m sine omega t और voltage है v m sine omega t, जहाँ omega equals two pi f, जो two pi over T भी है। ये तीन quantities, omega, f, और T, आपस में बदली जा सकती हैं, तो जो question कोई एक देता है वो असल में तीनों दे चुका है।

R M S values। I r m s equals i m divided by root two, यानी peak का nought point seven zero seven गुना, और voltage relation form में बिल्कुल वही है। Root two, two नहीं। यही एक फिसलन पूरे subtopic का सबसे common ग़लत जवाब है, तो अभी दर्ज कर लीजिए।

Half-cycle mean। I average equals two i m over pi, यानी peak का nought point six three seven गुना। Denominator में pi ध्यान दीजिए, ये half sine पर integration का fingerprint है, और वो integration हम दो section बाद देखेंगे।

दो ratios जो J E E Main नाम लेकर पूछता है। Form factor है R M S divided by half-cycle mean, जो निकलता है pi over two root two, यानी one point one one। Peak factor है peak divided by R M S, जो बस root two है, one point four one four। दोनों pure numbers हैं, कोई unit नहीं।

और जिस वजह से R M S बनी ही थी: resistor में average power। ये है I r m s squared times R, और उतना ही V r m s times I r m s, और उतना ही V r m s squared over R। इन तीनों forms को ध्यान से देखिए। ये exactly D C power formulas हैं जिनमें R M S values डाल दी गई हैं। ये संयोग नहीं, यही पूरा design goal था।

<excited> अब इस ladder को याद में जला लीजिए, क्योंकि ये यहाँ लिखे हर जवाब पर एक मुफ़्त error-check है। Half-cycle mean सबसे नीचे, peak का nought point six three seven। R M S उसके ऊपर, nought point seven zero seven। Peak सबसे ऊपर। Mean, फिर R M S, फिर peak, sinusoid के लिए हमेशा इसी क्रम में।

Mains numbers exam pressure में derive करने से बेहतर है सीधे याद कर लेना। Two hundred twenty volt R M S का peak है two hundred twenty root two, लगभग three hundred eleven volt। Fifty hertz का मतलब period nought point nought two second और omega one hundred pi, लगभग three hundred fourteen radian per second।

आख़िर में units, क्योंकि dimensional फिसलन आसान marks खा जाती है। Peak और R M S current दोनों ampere में, peak और R M S voltage दोनों volt में, क्योंकि R M S लेने से quantity की क़िस्म नहीं बदलती। Omega radian per second में। Form factor और peak factor एक जैसी quantities के ratio हैं, तो dimensionless।

sections.subtopic: AC Fundamentals: Average and RMS Values and Phasors
sections.title: Derivation: the RMS value of a sinusoidal current

board_events.text: Root of the mean of the square, done literally
The integral of sine squared is not standard, so convert it with the half-angle identity.

board_events.caption: Sine squared oscillates symmetrically about one half

board_events.text: Over one full period the sine term returns to zero, leaving only t = T.
Physical meaning: the average of sine squared over a cycle is exactly one half.

segments.text: This is the C B S E favourite, worth two to three marks almost every year, and it is nothing more than the name R M S carried out as instructions. Read the name backwards: square the current, take the mean, take the root.

So by definition, I r m s squared is the average of i squared over one full period. That average is written as one over T times the integral from zero to T of i squared d t, and with i equal to i m sine omega t, the thing under the integral is i m squared sine squared omega t.

Now we hit a small wall. The integral of sine squared is not a standard form you can write down by inspection. So we convert it into something we can integrate, and the tool for that is the half-angle identity.

Sine squared omega t equals one minus cosine two omega t, all over two. Look at what this has bought us. On the left is a squared function we cannot integrate directly. On the right is a constant plus a plain cosine, and both of those are trivial.

Substituting, I r m s squared becomes i m squared over T, times the integral of one minus cosine two omega t, over two, d t. Integrate term by term. The constant one gives t. The cosine gives sine two omega t divided by two omega. So we get i m squared over two T, times t minus sine two omega t over two omega, evaluated from zero to T.

Before we evaluate, look at the picture, because it shows the answer before the algebra does. This is sine squared plotted over a full period. It never goes negative, it oscillates between zero and one, and it is perfectly symmetric about the line at one half. Equal area above, equal area below. Its average is exactly one half.

The algebra confirms it. At the upper limit, two omega T is two full turns of the sine, so sine of it returns to zero. At the lower limit it is zero as well. The whole sine term vanishes at both ends and contributes nothing. Only the t term survives, giving T minus zero.

So I r m s squared equals i m squared over two T, multiplied by T. The T cancels, and we are left with i m squared over two. Take the square root and there it is: I r m s equals i m over root two. That is the derivation, complete, in five honest lines.

And now the physical reading, which is the sentence that earns the last mark. The mean of sine squared over a cycle is exactly one half, so the mean square current is i m squared over two. Its square root is the value that matches a D C current for heating, and that value is i m over root two.
ये C B S E का favourite है, लगभग हर साल दो से तीन marks का, और ये नाम R M S को instructions की तरह करने से ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं। नाम उल्टा पढ़िए: current को square कीजिए, mean लीजिए, root लीजिए।

तो definition से, I r m s squared है एक full period पर i squared का average। वो average लिखा जाता है one over T times integral zero से T तक i squared d t, और i equals i m sine omega t रखने पर integral के अंदर आता है i m squared sine squared omega t।
अब एक छोटी दीवार आती है। Sine squared का integral कोई standard form नहीं जो देखते ही लिख दें। तो हम इसे ऐसी चीज़ में बदलते हैं जिसे integrate कर सकें, और इसका tool है half-angle identity।

Sine squared omega t equals one minus cosine two omega t, पूरा two से divided। देखिए इसने क्या दिया। बाईं तरफ़ एक squared function है जिसे सीधे integrate नहीं कर सकते। दाईं तरफ़ एक constant plus एक सादा cosine है, और दोनों trivial हैं।

Substitute करने पर I r m s squared बनता है i m squared over T, times integral of one minus cosine two omega t, over two, d t। Term by term integrate कीजिए। Constant one देता है t। Cosine देता है sine two omega t divided by two omega। तो मिलता है i m squared over two T, times t minus sine two omega t over two omega, zero से T तक evaluate किया हुआ।

Evaluate करने से पहले picture देखिए, क्योंकि ये जवाब algebra से पहले दिखा देती है। ये sine squared है full period पर plot किया हुआ। ये कभी negative नहीं होता, zero और one के बीच oscillate करता है, और one half वाली line के बारे में perfectly symmetric है। ऊपर बराबर area, नीचे बराबर area। इसका average exactly one half है।

Algebra इसकी पुष्टि करती है। Upper limit पर two omega T sine के दो पूरे चक्कर हैं, तो उसका sine वापस zero पर आ जाता है। Lower limit पर भी zero है। पूरा sine term दोनों सिरों पर ग़ायब हो जाता है और कुछ contribute नहीं करता। सिर्फ़ t term बचता है, जो देता है T minus zero।

तो I r m s squared equals i m squared over two T, multiplied by T। T cancel हो जाता है, और बचता है i m squared over two। Square root लीजिए और यही है: I r m s equals i m over root two। यही derivation है, पूरा, पाँच ईमानदार lines में।

और अब physical reading, जो वो line है जिस पर आख़िरी mark मिलता है। Cycle पर sine squared का mean exactly one half है, तो mean square current है i m squared over two। उसका square root वो value है जो heating में D C current से मेल खाती है, और वो value है i m over root two।

sections.subtopic: AC Fundamentals: Average and RMS Values and Phasors
sections.title: Derivation: the mean value over a half cycle

board_events.text: The full cycle cancels, so average over the positive half only

board_events.caption: The positive half alone, whose area does not cancel

board_events.text: At the upper limit omega times T over 2 equals pi, and cos pi = -1 while cos 0 = +1.
Now close it with omega = 2 pi / T, so T times omega is exactly 2 pi.
RMS exceeds the half-cycle mean. Their ratio is the form factor, 1.11.

segments.text: The second derivation, and it is shorter than the first because there is no identity to hunt for. The only judgement call is choosing the limits, and that choice is forced on us by physics rather than by mathematics.

We already know the full-cycle average is zero, so averaging over the full period tells us nothing. Instead we average over the positive half alone, from zero to T over two. So I average equals one divided by T over two, times the integral from zero to T over two of i m sine omega t d t.

The picture is the whole idea in one glance. We are taking the area of that shaded positive hump and spreading it evenly over the half-period width. That is what an average is: total area divided by the interval. The negative hump is simply not invited.

Integrating sine omega t gives minus cosine omega t over omega. And one over T over two, the prefactor, is just two over T. So we have two i m over T, times minus cosine omega t over omega, evaluated from zero to T over two.

Now the key substitution, and this is where students most often stumble. At the upper limit, the argument omega times T over two. Since omega is two pi over T, that product is exactly pi. So we need cosine pi, which is minus one, and at the lower limit cosine zero, which is plus one.

Feed those in. We get two i m over T omega, times the bracket minus cosine pi plus cosine zero. That bracket is minus of minus one, plus one, which is one plus one, equal to two. So the expression becomes four i m divided by T omega.

One substitution left to close it. Omega equals two pi over T, so the product T omega is exactly two pi. Notice how neatly this works out. The period vanishes entirely, which it must, because a mean value cannot depend on how fast the wave happens to be running.

Therefore I average equals four i m over two pi, which simplifies to two i m over pi, or nought point six three seven times the peak. That is the half-cycle mean, and the pi in the denominator is the visible signature of the integration we just performed.

Compare it to the R M S value now, because examiners love the comparison. Nought point six three seven is smaller than nought point seven zero seven, so the R M S always exceeds the half-cycle mean. Divide one by the other and you get one point one one, which is the form factor, pi over two root two.
दूसरा derivation, और ये पहले से छोटा है क्योंकि कोई identity ढूँढ़नी नहीं पड़ती। एक ही judgement call है limits चुनना, और वो चुनाव physics थोपती है, mathematics नहीं।

हम जानते हैं full-cycle average zero है, तो पूरे period पर average लेना कुछ नहीं बताता। इसके बजाय हम सिर्फ़ positive half पर average लेते हैं, zero से T over two तक। तो I average equals one divided by T over two, times integral zero से T over two तक i m sine omega t d t।

Picture एक नज़र में पूरा idea है। हम उस shaded positive hump का area ले रहे हैं और उसे half-period की चौड़ाई पर बराबर फैला रहे हैं। Average यही होता है: कुल area divided by interval। Negative hump को बुलाया ही नहीं गया।

Sine omega t को integrate करने पर मिलता है minus cosine omega t over omega। और prefactor one over T over two बस two over T है। तो हमारे पास है two i m over T, times minus cosine omega t over omega, zero से T over two तक evaluate किया हुआ।

अब key substitution, और यहीं students सबसे ज़्यादा फिसलते हैं। Upper limit पर argument है omega times T over two। चूँकि omega है two pi over T, वो product exactly pi है। तो चाहिए cosine pi, जो minus one है, और lower limit पर cosine zero, जो plus one है।

इन्हें डालिए। मिलता है two i m over T omega, times bracket minus cosine pi plus cosine zero। वो bracket है minus of minus one, plus one, यानी one plus one, बराबर two। तो expression बनता है four i m divided by T omega।

बंद करने के लिए एक substitution बाकी। Omega equals two pi over T, तो product T omega exactly two pi है। देखिए ये कितनी सफ़ाई से बैठता है। Period पूरी तरह ग़ायब हो जाता है, और होना ही चाहिए, क्योंकि mean value इस पर depend नहीं कर सकती कि wave कितनी तेज़ चल रही है।

इसलिए I average equals four i m over two pi, जो simplify होकर two i m over pi बनता है, यानी peak का nought point six three seven गुना। यही half-cycle mean है, और denominator का pi उसी integration का दिखता हुआ हस्ताक्षर है जो हमने अभी किया।

अब इसे R M S value से compare कीजिए, क्योंकि examiners को यही comparison पसंद है। Nought point six three seven, nought point seven zero seven से छोटा है, तो R M S हमेशा half-cycle mean से बड़ा रहता है। एक को दूसरे से भाग दीजिए तो मिलता है one point one one, यानी form factor, pi over two root two।

sections.subtopic: AC Fundamentals: Average and RMS Values and Phasors
sections.title: Derivation: average power in a resistor, and why RMS is defined this way

board_events.text: The justification for the whole definition

board_events.latex: p = i^2 R = i_m^2 R \sin^2 \omega t

board_events.caption: Current alternates, but the power it delivers never turns negative

board_events.text: Instantaneous power is never negative, so unlike the current it cannot average to zero.
Identical in form to the DC result P = I squared R, provided the RMS current is used.
That equivalence is the entire reason RMS is defined the way it is.
Fast route for any resistor power question: P = half of i_m squared R.

segments.text: This third derivation is short, but it is the one that justifies everything. The previous two told us what R M S is. This one tells us why anybody bothered to define it that way in the first place.

Take a resistor carrying i equal to i m sine omega t. The instantaneous power it dissipates is i squared R, which expands to i m squared R sine squared omega t. Everything on the right is a constant except that sine squared factor, so the whole time-dependence of the power sits in one term.

The picture separates the two behaviours cleanly. On top, the current, swinging above and below the axis exactly as we expect. Underneath, the power, and look carefully: it never once goes below the axis. It touches zero when the current crosses zero, then rises again immediately, regardless of which direction the current is now heading.

That is the crucial asymmetry. The current averages to zero over a cycle because its two halves have opposite signs. The power cannot do that, because it is never negative in the first place. Notice too that the power peaks twice for every one current cycle, which is why energy questions often carry a factor of two in frequency.

Now we average. The only time-dependent piece is sine squared omega t, and we established its average in the R M S derivation: exactly one half. So the average power is i m squared R multiplied by one half.

Here is the elegant step. Write that one half as one over root two, all squared. Then i m squared times one half becomes i m over root two, the whole thing squared. And i m over root two is precisely our definition of I r m s. So the average power equals I r m s squared times R.

<excited> Stop and appreciate what just happened. P equals I squared R is the D C formula you have used since school. We have just shown that the A C average power obeys the identical formula, character for character, on the single condition that you feed it the R M S current.

And that is the whole reason R M S is defined the way it is. It was reverse-engineered to make A C power calculations look exactly like D C ones. Every other formula in this chapter that mixes voltages and currents inherits that convenience.

<whisper> One practical consequence worth carrying into the exam. Since average power is half of i m squared R, you can go straight from the peak current to the power without ever computing the R M S as a separate step. That one shortcut saves a line on almost every resistor power question you will meet.
ये तीसरा derivation छोटा है, पर यही सब कुछ justify करता है। पिछले दो ने बताया R M S है क्या। ये बताता है किसी ने इसे इस तरह define करने की ज़हमत क्यों उठाई।

एक resistor लीजिए जिसमें i equals i m sine omega t बह रहा है। जो instantaneous power वो dissipate करता है वो है i squared R, जो फैलकर बनता है i m squared R sine squared omega t। दाईं तरफ़ sine squared के अलावा सब constant है, तो power की पूरी time-dependence एक ही term में बैठी है।

Picture दोनों behaviours साफ़ अलग कर देती है। ऊपर current है, axis के ऊपर-नीचे झूलता हुआ, जैसी उम्मीद थी। नीचे power है, और ध्यान से देखिए: ये एक बार भी axis के नीचे नहीं जाती। Current zero पार करते समय ये zero छूती है, फिर तुरंत ऊपर उठ जाती है, चाहे current अब किसी भी direction में जा रहा हो।

यही निर्णायक asymmetry है। Current cycle पर zero average देता है क्योंकि उसके दो halves के sign उल्टे हैं। Power ऐसा नहीं कर सकती, क्योंकि वो कभी negative होती ही नहीं। ये भी देखिए कि power हर एक current cycle में दो बार peak करती है, इसीलिए energy वाले सवालों में frequency पर अक्सर दो का factor आता है।

अब average लेते हैं। इकलौता time-dependent टुकड़ा है sine squared omega t, और उसका average हमने R M S derivation में तय कर लिया था: exactly one half। तो average power है i m squared R multiplied by one half।

अब वो सुंदर क़दम। उस one half को लिखिए one over root two, पूरा squared। तब i m squared times one half बन जाता है i m over root two, पूरा squared। और i m over root two ठीक हमारी I r m s की definition है। तो average power equals I r m s squared times R।

<excited> रुककर देखिए अभी क्या हुआ। P equals I squared R वही D C formula है जो आप स्कूल से इस्तेमाल कर रहे हैं। हमने अभी दिखाया कि A C average power उसी formula को मानती है, अक्षर दर अक्षर, बस एक शर्त पर कि आप उसमें R M S current डालें।

और यही पूरी वजह है कि R M S इसी तरह define हुई। इसे उल्टा design किया गया ताकि A C power calculations बिल्कुल D C जैसी दिखें। इस chapter का हर दूसरा formula जो voltage और current मिलाता है, वही सुविधा विरासत में पाता है।

<whisper> एक practical नतीजा exam में ले जाने लायक़। चूँकि average power है half of i m squared R, आप peak current से सीधे power पर पहुँच सकते हैं, R M S को अलग step में निकाले बिना। यही एक shortcut resistor power के लगभग हर सवाल में एक line बचा देता है।

board_events.text: CBSE Board Level
The peak voltage of a sinusoidal AC supply is 311 V. Find (a) the rms voltage and (b) the mean voltage over a half cycle.

board_events.text: 220 V. The familiar mains rating falls straight out.
Answer: V_rms = 220 V and V_avg = 198 V.
RMS always exceeds the half-cycle mean. Their ratio is the form factor, 1.11.

segments.text: A clean board-level opener. We are handed the peak voltage of a sinusoidal supply, three hundred eleven volts, and asked for two things: the r m s voltage, and the mean voltage over a half cycle.

Read the question carefully first, because the wording is doing real work. It says peak, explicitly. That is unusual and generous, because most questions hand you the r m s value and expect you to know it. Here the peak is given, so both remaining quantities are one substitution away.

The picture shows what we are actually computing. One supply, three descriptions. The tall red bar is the peak, three hundred eleven volts. The blue bar is what we are about to find for part a, and the green bar is part b. Same supply, three honest numbers, and they are not interchangeable.
So, given: v m equals three hundred eleven volts. That is the only data we have, and it is enough.
Part a. V r m s equals v m divided by root two, which is three hundred eleven divided by one point four one four. Work that through and you get two hundred twenty volts.

<excited> And there is the number on every socket in the country. Notice what this tells you about your own home: the mains you call two hundred twenty volts is a sine wave that actually peaks at three hundred eleven volts, twice in every cycle, fifty times a second.

Part b. The half-cycle mean is two v m over pi, so that is two times three hundred eleven, divided by three point one four one six. That gives one hundred ninety eight volts. Notice the two in the numerator; forgetting it is the standard slip here and lands you at ninety nine.
So the answers are two hundred twenty volts for the r m s and one hundred ninety eight volts for the half-cycle mean.

Now check them against the ladder before you move on. One hundred ninety eight is less than two hundred twenty, which is less than three hundred eleven. Mean below r m s below peak, exactly as required. And divide two hundred twenty by one hundred ninety eight and you get one point one one, the form factor. The answer checks itself.
एक साफ़ board-level शुरुआत। हमें sinusoidal supply का peak voltage दिया गया है, three hundred eleven volt, और दो चीज़ें पूछी हैं: r m s voltage, और half cycle पर mean voltage।

पहले question ध्यान से पढ़िए, क्योंकि उसके शब्द असली काम कर रहे हैं। वो साफ़ लिखता है peak। ये असामान्य और उदार है, क्योंकि ज़्यादातर questions r m s देते हैं और उम्मीद करते हैं आपको पता हो। यहाँ peak दिया है, तो बाकी दोनों quantities एक substitution दूर हैं।

Picture दिखाती है हम असल में क्या निकाल रहे हैं। एक supply, तीन descriptions। ऊँचा लाल bar peak है, three hundred eleven volt। नीला bar वो है जो हम part a में निकालने वाले हैं, और हरा bar part b है। वही supply, तीन ईमानदार numbers, और ये आपस में बदले नहीं जा सकते।
तो दिया है: v m equals three hundred eleven volt। यही इकलौता data है, और यही काफ़ी है।
Part a। V r m s equals v m divided by root two, यानी three hundred eleven divided by one point four one four। हल कीजिए तो मिलता है two hundred twenty volt।

<excited> और यही वो number है जो देश के हर socket पर लिखा है। ध्यान दीजिए ये आपके घर के बारे में क्या बताता है: जिस mains को आप two hundred twenty volt कहते हैं, वो असल में three hundred eleven volt तक चढ़ती है, हर cycle में दो बार, एक second में पचास बार।

Part b। Half-cycle mean है two v m over pi, यानी two times three hundred eleven, divided by three point one four one six। मिलता है one hundred ninety eight volt। Numerator में two ध्यान दीजिए; उसे भूलना यहाँ की standard फिसलन है और आपको ninety nine पर ले जाती है।
तो जवाब हैं r m s के लिए two hundred twenty volt और half-cycle mean के लिए one hundred ninety eight volt।

अब आगे बढ़ने से पहले इन्हें ladder पर जाँचिए। One hundred ninety eight, two hundred twenty से कम है, जो three hundred eleven से कम है। Mean नीचे, r m s बीच में, peak ऊपर, ठीक जैसा चाहिए। और two hundred twenty को one hundred ninety eight से भाग दीजिए तो मिलता है one point one one, यानी form factor। जवाब ख़ुद को जाँच लेता है।

sections.subtopic: AC Fundamentals: Average and RMS Values and Phasors
sections.title: Worked example: what does a 220 V label actually promise?

board_events.text: NEET Speed Trap
An AC source is labelled 220 V. What is its peak voltage?
The trap: assuming 220 V is the peak. It is not.

board_events.caption: The label reports the rms; the wave still reaches the peak

board_events.text: Every AC rating is an rms value unless the word peak appears explicitly.
Answer: 311 V.
Home wiring insulation must survive 311 V, not 220 V. A favourite one-mark trap.
Rate by RMS, build for the peak.

segments.text: This one is deliberately short, because in N E E T you will have well under a minute for it. An A C source is labelled two hundred twenty volts. Find its peak voltage.

The trap is set in the word labelled, and it catches students who are moving fast. The instinct is to treat the printed number as the biggest value the source ever reaches, and therefore as the peak. It is not the peak.

Here is what the label actually describes. The blue curve is the real voltage in your wall. The green line is where the label sits, at two hundred twenty. The red line, noticeably higher, is where the wave genuinely reaches. The label is reporting the r m s, the heating-equivalent value, not the crest.

So commit this rule to memory as a reflex, because it recurs across the whole chapter. Every A C rating you meet is an r m s value, unless the question explicitly uses the word peak. Meters read r m s. Appliance plates quote r m s. Exam questions default to r m s.

Now the arithmetic, which is trivial once the concept is right. Since r m s equals peak over root two, the peak must be r m s times root two. That is two hundred twenty times one point four one four, which is about three hundred eleven volts.

Watch the direction of the operation, because this is where the marks are actually lost. If you are given the r m s and want the peak, you multiply by root two. If you are given the peak and want the r m s, you divide. Getting this backwards turns three hundred eleven into one hundred fifty six, and both numbers will look plausible under time pressure.
So the answer is three hundred eleven volts.

<whisper> And here is the detail the examiner is really testing, dressed as a physics fact about your own house. The insulation in your home wiring is not protecting against two hundred twenty volts. It has to survive three hundred eleven volts, a hundred times every second. Engineers size insulation to the peak, always.

Carry that as a single sentence: rate by r m s, build for the peak. Ratings, bills, and meter readings live in the r m s world. Insulation, breakdown, and component voltage limits live in the peak world. Ask which world the question is in before you reach for root two.
ये जानबूझकर छोटा है, क्योंकि N E E T में इसके लिए एक मिनट से कम मिलेगा। एक A C source पर लिखा है two hundred twenty volt। इसका peak voltage निकालिए।
जाल labelled शब्द में बिछा है, और वो तेज़ी से भागते students को पकड़ता है। Instinct होती है कि छपे हुए number को source की सबसे बड़ी value मान लें, यानी peak। वो peak नहीं है।

ये रहा वो जो label असल में बताता है। नीली curve आपकी दीवार का असली voltage है। हरी line वहाँ है जहाँ label बैठा है, two hundred twenty पर। लाल line, साफ़ ऊपर, वहाँ है जहाँ wave सचमुच पहुँचती है। Label r m s बता रहा है, heating-equivalent value, crest नहीं।

तो इस नियम को reflex बना लीजिए, क्योंकि ये पूरे chapter में लौटकर आता है। आपको मिलने वाली हर A C rating r m s value है, जब तक question साफ़ शब्दों में peak न लिखे। Meter r m s पढ़ते हैं। Appliance plate r m s लिखते हैं। Exam questions default में r m s मानते हैं।

अब arithmetic, जो concept सही होते ही मामूली है। चूँकि r m s equals peak over root two, तो peak होगा r m s times root two। यानी two hundred twenty times one point four one four, लगभग three hundred eleven volt।

Operation की direction देखिए, क्योंकि असली marks यहीं कटते हैं। अगर r m s दिया है और peak चाहिए, तो root two से गुणा। अगर peak दिया है और r m s चाहिए, तो भाग। इसे उल्टा करने पर three hundred eleven, one hundred fifty six बन जाता है, और time pressure में दोनों numbers जायज़ लगेंगे।
तो जवाब है three hundred eleven volt।

<whisper> और ये रही वो बात जो examiner असल में जाँच रहा है, आपके अपने घर के physics fact के भेस में। आपकी घरेलू wiring का insulation two hundred twenty volt से नहीं बचा रहा। उसे three hundred eleven volt झेलना पड़ता है, हर second सौ बार। Engineers insulation हमेशा peak के हिसाब से चुनते हैं।

इसे एक line में साथ रखिए: rate by r m s, build for the peak। Ratings, bills और meter readings r m s की दुनिया में रहते हैं। Insulation, breakdown और component voltage limits peak की दुनिया में। Root two उठाने से पहले पूछिए कि question किस दुनिया में है।

sections.subtopic: AC Fundamentals: Average and RMS Values and Phasors
sections.title: Worked example: frequency, RMS and power from a waveform

board_events.text: JEE Main Level
A current i = 4 sin(100 pi t) A flows through a 100 ohm resistor. Find (a) the frequency, (b) the rms current, (c) the average power.

board_events.caption: Reading the peak and the angular frequency straight off the waveform

board_events.latex: \text{Compare with } i = i_m \sin\omega t \;\Rightarrow\; i_m = 4\ \text{A},\quad \omega = 100\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}

board_events.text: Shortcut: P = half of i_m squared R = half of 16 times 100 = 800 W. The half is the RMS factor squared.
Answer: f = 50 Hz, I_rms = 2.83 A, P_avg = 800 W.

segments.text: Now a J E E Main level problem, and the skill it tests is not really algebra. It is reading a waveform expression correctly. A current, i equals four sine of one hundred pi t amperes, flows through a one hundred ohm resistor. We want the frequency, the r m s current, and the average power.

Everything you need is already sitting in that expression, so the first move is always the same: compare it, term by term, with the standard form i equals i m sine omega t. Do not skip this step even when it feels obvious, because it is where the given data actually gets unpacked.

The picture shows what the comparison extracts. The number in front of the sine sets the height of the curve, that is the peak, four amperes. The number multiplying t inside the sine sets how fast it oscillates, that is omega, one hundred pi radians per second. Two numbers, two completely different roles.

So the comparison gives i m equals four amperes and omega equals one hundred pi radians per second. Notice that the resistance played no part here at all. It is not in the waveform, and it will only enter in the final part.

Part a, the frequency. Omega is two pi f, so f is omega over two pi, which is one hundred pi divided by two pi. The pi cancels immediately, leaving one hundred over two, which is fifty hertz. And that should feel reassuring, because one hundred pi is exactly the Indian mains angular frequency.

Part b, the r m s current. The peak is four amperes, so I r m s is four over root two, which is two point eight three amperes. You can also read this as four divided by one point four one four, or as two root two, whichever you find faster under pressure.

Part c, the average power. Only the resistor dissipates, and the formula is I r m s squared times R. That is two point eight three squared, which is eight, multiplied by one hundred ohms. So the average power is eight hundred watts.

<excited> But watch this faster route, because on a timed paper it matters. Average power is half of i m squared times R. That is half of sixteen times one hundred, which is eight hundred watts directly. You never computed the r m s at all. That one half is nothing but the r m s factor squared, hiding in plain sight.

So the answers: fifty hertz, two point eight three amperes, and eight hundred watts. Do one last sanity pass. The r m s, two point eight three, sits below the peak of four, as it must. And the power came out positive and finite. Both boxes ticked.

अब एक J E E Main level problem, और ये असल में algebra नहीं जाँच रहा। ये waveform expression सही पढ़ना जाँच रहा है। एक current, i equals four sine of one hundred pi t ampere, एक one hundred ohm resistor से बह रहा है। चाहिए frequency, r m s current, और average power।

जो चाहिए वो सब उसी expression में बैठा है, तो पहला क़दम हमेशा एक ही है: इसे term by term standard form i equals i m sine omega t से compare कीजिए। ये step obvious लगने पर भी मत छोड़िए, क्योंकि दिया हुआ data यहीं खुलता है।

Picture दिखाती है comparison क्या निकालती है। Sine के आगे का number curve की ऊँचाई तय करता है, वो है peak, four ampere। Sine के अंदर t से गुणा होने वाला number तय करता है कि ये कितनी तेज़ oscillate करती है, वो है omega, one hundred pi radian per second। दो numbers, दो बिल्कुल अलग भूमिकाएँ।

तो comparison देता है i m equals four ampere और omega equals one hundred pi radian per second। ध्यान दीजिए resistance की यहाँ कोई भूमिका नहीं थी। वो waveform में है ही नहीं, और सिर्फ़ आख़िरी part में आएगा।

Part a, frequency। Omega है two pi f, तो f है omega over two pi, यानी one hundred pi divided by two pi। Pi तुरंत cancel हो जाता है, बचता है one hundred over two, यानी fifty hertz। और ये तसल्ली देने वाला होना चाहिए, क्योंकि one hundred pi ठीक Indian mains की angular frequency है।

Part b, r m s current। Peak है four ampere, तो I r m s है four over root two, यानी two point eight three ampere। इसे four divided by one point four one four भी पढ़ सकते हैं, या two root two, जो pressure में तेज़ लगे।

Part c, average power। सिर्फ़ resistor dissipate करता है, और formula है I r m s squared times R। यानी two point eight three squared, जो eight है, multiplied by one hundred ohm। तो average power है eight hundred watt।

<excited> पर ये तेज़ रास्ता देखिए, क्योंकि timed paper में यही matter करता है। Average power है half of i m squared times R। यानी half of sixteen times one hundred, सीधे eight hundred watt। आपने r m s निकाला ही नहीं। वो one half और कुछ नहीं, r m s factor का square है, सामने ही छिपा हुआ।

तो जवाब: fifty hertz, two point eight three ampere, और eight hundred watt। एक आख़िरी sanity pass कीजिए। r m s, two point eight three, four के peak से नीचे बैठा है, जैसा होना चाहिए। और power positive और finite निकली। दोनों डिब्बे tick।

sections.subtopic: AC Fundamentals: Average and RMS Values and Phasors
sections.title: Worked example: RMS of a DC current with AC riding on top

board_events.text: JEE Advanced Level
A current i = (3 + 4 sin(omega t)) A flows through a 5 ohm resistor. Find (a) the rms current, (b) the average power.

board_events.caption: A steady 3 A floor with a 4 A peak ripple riding on it

board_events.text: Average term by term: the constant survives, the bare sine dies, the sine squared gives half.
Mean squares add: 3 squared plus (4 over root 2) squared = 9 + 8 = 17.
The DC part and the AC part heat independently. The cross term averages away.

segments.text: This is the Advanced-level version, and it punishes anyone who has memorised the root two factor without understanding where it came from. A current of three plus four sine omega t amperes, a steady three amperes with a four ampere peak ripple riding on top, flows through a five ohm resistor.

Look at the picture first, because it makes the physical situation unambiguous. The green dashed line is the steady three ampere floor. The blue wave oscillates about that floor, not about zero. So the current swings between minus one and seven amperes, and it is never a pure sine.

That is exactly why the root two shortcut is illegal here. Dividing four by root two would give you the r m s of the ripple alone, and dividing seven by root two is meaningless. The factor belongs to a pure sinusoid, and this is not one. We must go back to the definition.

So return to first principles. R m s means the root of the mean of i squared. Square the current honestly: three plus four sine omega t, all squared, expands to nine, plus twenty four sine omega t, plus sixteen sine squared omega t. Three terms, and we now average each one separately.

Take them one at a time. The nine is a constant, so its average over a cycle is just nine. The twenty four sine omega t term is a bare sine, and we established in the very first section that a full-cycle average of a sine is exactly zero, so this term dies completely. And sixteen sine squared averages to sixteen times one half, which is eight.
Adding those up, the mean of i squared is nine plus zero plus eight, which is seventeen. The r m s current is therefore the square root of seventeen, about four point one two amperes.

Part b follows immediately, and notice we do not need to take the square root at all. Average power is I r m s squared times R, and I r m s squared is exactly seventeen, sitting right there before we rooted it. So the power is seventeen times five, which is eighty five watts.

<excited> Now the deep idea this problem exists to teach. Look at the structure of that seventeen. It is nine plus eight, which is three squared plus four over root two, squared. In other words, the mean square of the D C part plus the mean square of the A C part. Mean squares add.

Physically, that means the D C part and the A C part heat the resistor completely independently, and the cross term between them, our twenty four sine, contributes nothing over a full cycle. Carry the rule forward in this exact form: never add r m s values, add their squares.

ये Advanced-level version है, और ये उन्हें सज़ा देता है जिन्होंने root two factor रट लिया है पर ये नहीं समझा कि वो आया कहाँ से। तीन plus four sine omega t ampere का current, यानी steady three ampere पर सवार four ampere peak की ripple, एक five ohm resistor से बह रहा है।

पहले picture देखिए, क्योंकि वो physical situation साफ़ कर देती है। हरी dashed line steady three ampere का फ़र्श है। नीली wave उसी फ़र्श के इर्द-गिर्द झूलती है, zero के नहीं। तो current minus one से seven ampere के बीच झूलता है, और ये कभी pure sine नहीं है।

और ठीक इसीलिए root two वाला shortcut यहाँ नाजायज़ है। Four को root two से भाग देने पर सिर्फ़ ripple का r m s मिलेगा, और seven को root two से भाग देना बेमानी है। वो factor pure sinusoid का है, और ये pure sinusoid नहीं। हमें definition पर लौटना होगा।

तो first principles पर वापस। R m s का मतलब है root of the mean of i squared। Current को ईमानदारी से square कीजिए: three plus four sine omega t, पूरा squared, फैलकर बनता है nine, plus twenty four sine omega t, plus sixteen sine squared omega t। तीन terms, और अब हर एक का अलग average लेंगे।

एक-एक करके लीजिए। Nine constant है, तो cycle पर उसका average nine ही है। Twenty four sine omega t वाला term सादा sine है, और पहले ही section में तय हुआ था कि sine का full-cycle average exactly zero है, तो ये term पूरा मर जाता है। और sixteen sine squared का average है sixteen times one half, यानी eight।
जोड़िए तो i squared का mean है nine plus zero plus eight, यानी seventeen। इसलिए r m s current है square root of seventeen, लगभग four point one two ampere।

Part b तुरंत निकल आता है, और ध्यान दीजिए square root लेने की ज़रूरत ही नहीं। Average power है I r m s squared times R, और I r m s squared exactly seventeen है, root लेने से पहले ही सामने पड़ा था। तो power है seventeen times five, यानी eighty five watt।

<excited> अब वो गहरा idea जिसके लिए ये problem बनी है। उस seventeen की बनावट देखिए। वो nine plus eight है, यानी three squared plus four over root two, squared। दूसरे शब्दों में, D C हिस्से का mean square plus A C हिस्से का mean square। Mean squares जुड़ते हैं।

Physically इसका मतलब है D C हिस्सा और A C हिस्सा resistor को बिल्कुल स्वतंत्र रूप से गरम करते हैं, और उनके बीच का cross term, हमारा twenty four sine, full cycle पर कुछ contribute नहीं करता। इस नियम को इसी रूप में आगे ले जाइए: r m s values कभी मत जोड़िए, उनके squares जोड़िए।

board_events.text: Common student pitfalls

board_events.caption: Four wrong reflexes and their corrections

board_events.text: 1. Treating the rated voltage as the peak. 220 V mains is rms; the peak is 311 V.
Every AC rating you meet is RMS unless it explicitly says peak.
2. Saying the average of AC is something non-zero. Over a full cycle it is exactly zero.
3. Applying the root-2 factor to non-sinusoids. For a square wave I_rms = i_m.
For any other shape you must integrate the mean of i squared from scratch.
4. Forgetting that mean squares add, not rms values.

board_events.latex: I_{rms}^2 = I_1^2 + I_2^2 + \dots \quad\text{(cross terms average to zero)}

segments.text: Before we leave this subtopic, let us collect the four mistakes that actually cost marks. These are not exotic. They are the reflexes that fire when you are tired, and every one of them has a matching correction.
The grid pairs each wrong reflex with what is actually true. Red on top, correction in green underneath. If you can reproduce this grid from memory, the whole subtopic is secure.

First trap: treating the rated voltage as the peak. Two hundred twenty volt mains is an r m s value, and its peak is three hundred eleven volts. Students lose the mark by plugging two hundred twenty in wherever v m belongs.

The fix is a blanket rule with no exceptions to remember. Every A C rating you meet is r m s unless the word peak is printed. Meters, appliance plates, exam data, all r m s by default. To go up to the peak, multiply by root two.

Second trap: claiming the average of an alternating current is some non-zero number. Over a full cycle it is exactly zero, not approximately zero, not small. Only the half-cycle mean, two i m over pi, is non-zero, and you must say which one you mean.

Third trap, and this is the one that separates the top scorers. The root two factor is specific to sine waves. It came out of integrating sine squared, so it belongs to sine and nothing else. For a square wave the current sits at full magnitude the entire time, so its r m s equals the peak itself.

For any other shape, a triangular wave, a rectified wave, a trapezoid, there is no factor to look up. You go back to the definition and integrate the mean of i squared from scratch. Slow, but it is the only honest route.
Fourth trap: adding r m s values directly when several currents are present. That is wrong for the same reason we saw in the last example. R m s values do not add. Their squares do.

<whisper> So the correct statement is that I r m s squared equals I one squared plus I two squared and so on, because the cross terms between differently behaving components average to zero over a cycle. Write it down as a squares equation and you will never mis-handle a mixed waveform again.
इस subtopic को छोड़ने से पहले उन चार ग़लतियों को इकट्ठा कर लेते हैं जो सचमुच marks खाती हैं। ये कोई अनोखी नहीं हैं। ये वो reflexes हैं जो थकान में चल जाते हैं, और हर एक के साथ उसका सुधार भी है।
Grid हर ग़लत reflex को उसके सच के साथ जोड़ती है। ऊपर लाल में ग़लती, नीचे हरे में सुधार। अगर आप ये grid याद से बना सकते हैं, तो पूरा subtopic सुरक्षित है।

पहला जाल: rated voltage को peak मान लेना। Two hundred twenty volt mains एक r m s value है, और उसका peak three hundred eleven volt है। Students वहाँ two hundred twenty डालकर mark गँवाते हैं जहाँ v m आना चाहिए।

इसका इलाज एक बेशर्त नियम है, कोई अपवाद याद नहीं रखना। आपको मिलने वाली हर A C rating r m s है, जब तक peak शब्द छपा न हो। Meters, appliance plate, exam data, सब default में r m s। Peak तक जाने के लिए root two से गुणा।

दूसरा जाल: कहना कि alternating current का average कोई non-zero number है। Full cycle पर वो exactly zero है, लगभग zero नहीं, छोटा नहीं। सिर्फ़ half-cycle mean, two i m over pi, non-zero है, और आपको बताना होगा कौन सा वाला।

तीसरा जाल, और यही top scorers को अलग करता है। Root two factor sine waves के लिए ही है। वो sine squared को integrate करने से निकला था, तो वो sine का है और किसी का नहीं। Square wave में current पूरे समय full magnitude पर बैठा रहता है, तो उसका r m s peak के बराबर होता है।

किसी और shape के लिए, triangular wave, rectified wave, trapezoid, कोई factor देखने को नहीं है। आप definition पर लौटिए और i squared के mean को शुरू से integrate कीजिए। धीमा है, पर यही इकलौता ईमानदार रास्ता है।
चौथा जाल: कई currents होने पर r m s values सीधे जोड़ देना। ये उसी वजह से ग़लत है जो पिछले example में दिखी। R m s values नहीं जुड़तीं। उनके squares जुड़ते हैं।

<whisper> तो सही कथन ये है कि I r m s squared equals I one squared plus I two squared वग़ैरह, क्योंकि अलग व्यवहार वाले components के बीच के cross terms cycle पर zero average देते हैं। इसे squares के समीकरण की तरह लिखिए और mixed waveform फिर कभी ग़लत नहीं होगा।

board_events.text: RMS must always sit between the half-cycle mean and the peak: 0.637 i_m, then 0.707 i_m, then i_m.
If your rms lands outside that window for a sinusoid, you have slipped somewhere.

segments.text: Two pro-tips to close the subtopic. The first saves you time on every power question, and the second catches your errors before the examiner does.

Start with speed. Whenever a question asks for average power dissipated in a resistor and hands you peak values, do not walk the long path of computing the r m s first and then squaring it. Go directly.

The direct formula is P equals one half v m i m, and equivalently one half i m squared R. Those peak values are usually exactly what the question gave you, so this is a single substitution with no intermediate step to get wrong.

The picture shows why this is legitimate rather than a memory trick. That one half is not an arbitrary constant. It is one over root two, squared, which is the r m s factor with its square already taken. The r m s conversion is still happening; it is just baked into the formula, so you never write it down.

So on a timed paper, when you see a peak current and a resistance, the entire answer is half, times the peak squared, times R. One line. Reserve the longer route for questions that actually ask for the r m s as a separate part.
Now the second tip, which costs no time at all and is worth more than it looks: a sanity check you can run on any sinusoidal answer.

The ladder gives you the fixed ordering. The half-cycle mean sits at nought point six three seven of the peak. The r m s sits above it at nought point seven zero seven. The peak sits on top. That order is not negotiable for a sinusoid; it comes straight from the two integrals we derived.

So whenever you compute an r m s value, glance at it against that window. It must be larger than the half-cycle mean and smaller than the peak. If your r m s comes out above the peak, you multiplied by root two when you should have divided, and if it comes out below the mean, something worse has happened.

<chuckle> That check takes about two seconds and it has rescued more marks than any formula on this board. Run it every single time, especially in the last few minutes when you are moving fast and your arithmetic is the least trustworthy.
Subtopic बंद करने के लिए दो pro-tips। पहला हर power question में समय बचाता है, और दूसरा आपकी ग़लतियाँ examiner से पहले पकड़ लेता है।
Speed से शुरू। जब भी question resistor में average power पूछे और peak values दे, तो पहले r m s निकालकर फिर square करने का लंबा रास्ता मत लीजिए। सीधे जाइए।

सीधा formula है P equals one half v m i m, और उतना ही one half i m squared R। वो peak values आमतौर पर वही होती हैं जो question ने दी हैं, तो ये एक ही substitution है, बीच में ग़लत होने के लिए कोई step ही नहीं।

Picture दिखाती है ये जायज़ क्यों है, कोई याददाश्त की चाल नहीं। वो one half कोई मनमाना constant नहीं है। वो one over root two, squared है, यानी r m s factor जिसका square पहले ही ले लिया गया। R m s conversion अब भी हो रही है; बस formula में पक चुकी है, तो आप उसे लिखते ही नहीं।
तो timed paper में जब peak current और resistance दिखे, पूरा जवाब है half, times peak squared, times R। एक line। लंबा रास्ता उन्हीं questions के लिए बचाइए जो r m s अलग से पूछते हैं।
अब दूसरा tip, जो समय बिल्कुल नहीं लेता और दिखने से ज़्यादा क़ीमती है: एक sanity check जो आप किसी भी sinusoidal जवाब पर चला सकते हैं।

Ladder आपको तय क्रम देती है। Half-cycle mean peak के nought point six three seven पर बैठा है। R m s उसके ऊपर nought point seven zero seven पर। Peak सबसे ऊपर। Sinusoid के लिए ये क्रम बदल नहीं सकता; ये सीधे उन्हीं दो integrals से आता है जो हमने derive किए।

तो जब भी r m s value निकालें, उसे इस window के against एक नज़र देख लीजिए। वो half-cycle mean से बड़ी और peak से छोटी होनी चाहिए। अगर r m s peak से ऊपर निकली, तो आपने root two से गुणा किया जहाँ भाग करना था, और अगर mean से नीचे निकली, तो कुछ और भी बुरा हुआ है।

<chuckle> ये जाँच लगभग दो second लेती है और इसने इस board के किसी भी formula से ज़्यादा marks बचाए हैं। हर बार चलाइए, ख़ासकर आख़िरी कुछ minutes में जब आप तेज़ चल रहे होते हैं और आपकी arithmetic सबसे कम भरोसेमंद होती है।

board_events.text: The resistor is indifferent: it moves with the crowd, so voltage and current stay in step.
The inductor hates changes in current. Its current always lags the voltage.
The capacitor hates steady current. Its current always leads the voltage.

board_events.caption: The same voltage, three different current responses

board_events.text: Each opposes AC in a way that depends on how fast the current is swinging.
So opposition in AC has a size AND a timing.

segments.text: <curious> In a D C circuit, opposition to current has exactly one face, and its name is resistance. You push with a steady voltage, you get a steady current, and Ohm law settles the whole argument in a single line.

Alternating current changes the game, because the driving voltage is no longer steady. It swings sinusoidally, fifty times every second. And the moment the push starts oscillating, two new characters walk on stage who were invisible in D C.

Picture a crowded Mumbai local turnstile at rush hour, with the crowd surging forward and ebbing back rhythmically. That surge is our alternating drive. Three commuters are trying to get through, and each one responds to the same crowd completely differently.

The resistor is the steady, indifferent commuter. Whatever the crowd does, they simply move with it. Surge forward when the crowd surges, ebb back when it ebbs, no hesitation and no anticipation. Voltage and current stay perfectly in step, and we say they are in phase.

The inductor is the cautious uncle who resists any sudden change of motion. By the time he has committed to moving forward, the crowd has already peaked and started back. So his motion, which is the current, always arrives after the push. The current lags the voltage.

The capacitor is the over-eager teenager who lunges ahead before the crowd has even committed. The current through a capacitor is already flowing hard while the voltage is still climbing from zero. The current leads the voltage.

The second picture makes this concrete. The same solid voltage curve drives all three, and the dashed curve is the current in each case. For the resistor, the two curves rise and fall together. For the inductor, the dashed current is shifted to the right, arriving a quarter cycle late. For the capacitor, it is shifted left, arriving a quarter cycle early.

And there is a second, equally important difference between them. Each of these three opposes A C, but the inductor and the capacitor do it in a way that depends on how fast the current is swinging, which is to say on the frequency. The resistor alone is indifferent to frequency.

So here is the shift in thinking that this whole subtopic demands. In D C, opposition was one number. In A C, opposition has two properties: a size, telling you how much current you get, and a timing, telling you when that current arrives relative to the push. Both matter, and neither can be ignored.

<curious> D C circuit में current के विरोध का बस एक चेहरा होता है, और उसका नाम है resistance। आप steady voltage से push करते हैं, steady current मिलता है, और Ohm law पूरी बहस एक line में निपटा देता है।

Alternating current खेल बदल देता है, क्योंकि driving voltage अब steady नहीं है। वो sinusoidally झूलता है, हर second पचास बार। और जैसे ही push oscillate करने लगता है, दो नए किरदार stage पर आ जाते हैं जो D C में अदृश्य थे।

Rush hour में Mumbai local का भीड़ भरा turnstile सोचिए, जहाँ भीड़ लयबद्ध ढंग से आगे बढ़ती और पीछे हटती है। वही surge हमारा alternating drive है। तीन commuters निकलने की कोशिश कर रहे हैं, और हर एक उसी भीड़ पर बिल्कुल अलग प्रतिक्रिया देता है।

Resistor वो steady, उदासीन commuter है। भीड़ जो भी करे, वो बस उसके साथ चलता है। भीड़ बढ़े तो आगे, हटे तो पीछे, न झिझक न पूर्वानुमान। Voltage और current perfectly साथ चलते हैं, और हम कहते हैं वो in phase हैं।

Inductor वो सतर्क चाचा है जो गति के किसी भी अचानक बदलाव का विरोध करता है। जब तक वो आगे बढ़ने का मन बनाता है, भीड़ peak करके वापस मुड़ चुकी होती है। तो उसकी गति, यानी current, हमेशा push के बाद आती है। Current voltage से lag करता है।

Capacitor वो उतावला teenager है जो भीड़ के तय करने से पहले ही छलाँग लगा देता है। Capacitor में current तब ही ज़ोर से बह रहा होता है जब voltage अभी zero से ऊपर चढ़ ही रहा है। Current voltage से lead करता है।

दूसरी picture इसे ठोस बना देती है। वही ठोस voltage curve तीनों को चला रही है, और dashed curve हर case का current है। Resistor में दोनों curves साथ उठती-गिरती हैं। Inductor में dashed current दाईं तरफ़ खिसका है, एक चौथाई cycle देर से आता हुआ। Capacitor में बाईं तरफ़, एक चौथाई cycle पहले।

और इनमें एक दूसरा, उतना ही अहम फ़र्क़ है। ये तीनों A C का विरोध करते हैं, पर inductor और capacitor ये विरोध इस बात पर निर्भर करके करते हैं कि current कितनी तेज़ी से झूल रहा है, यानी frequency पर। अकेला resistor ही frequency के प्रति उदासीन है।

तो ये रहा सोच का वो बदलाव जो ये पूरा subtopic माँगता है। D C में विरोध एक number था। A C में विरोध की दो properties हैं: एक size, जो बताती है कितना current मिलेगा, और एक timing, जो बताती है वो current push के मुक़ाबले कब पहुँचेगा। दोनों matter करते हैं, किसी को नज़रअंदाज़ नहीं किया जा सकता।

sections.subtopic: AC Voltage across R, L, C and LCR Series Circuits
sections.title: Reactance: opposition that changes with frequency

board_events.text: Frequency-dependent opposition has a name: reactance, X

board_events.latex: X_L = \omega L \quad\text{(grows with frequency)}, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} \quad\text{(falls with frequency)}

board_events.caption: Inductive reactance rises while capacitive reactance falls

board_events.text: Unlike resistance, reactance stores and returns energy instead of dissipating it.
But dimensionally and operationally it behaves just like resistance. Same unit: the ohm.
Faster swings mean the inductor is asked to change direction more violently, so it digs in harder.
A capacitor likes rapid reversal. A steady push leaves it fully charged and blocking everything.
DC limits: an inductor becomes a short circuit, a capacitor becomes an open circuit.
Two opposite trends must cross somewhere. That crossing is resonance.

segments.text: That frequency-dependent opposition deserves a proper name, and it has one. It is called reactance, written with a capital X, and it is what an inductor or a capacitor offers instead of resistance.

The two reactances are beautifully simple to write and exactly opposite in behaviour. Inductive reactance X L equals omega L, so it grows in direct proportion to frequency. Capacitive reactance X C equals one over omega C, so it falls as frequency rises. One climbs, one collapses.

The graph makes the opposition unmistakable. The blue straight line is X L, rising steadily from the origin. The red curve is X C, starting enormous at low frequency and dropping away. Because one rises and the other falls, they are guaranteed to cross at exactly one frequency, marked in green. Remember that crossing point; two subtopics from now it will be the whole story of resonance.

Now a genuinely important distinction. Reactance is not resistance wearing a different hat. A resistor takes electrical energy and turns it irreversibly into heat. A reactance does not dissipate anything at all. It takes energy in during one part of the cycle, stores it in a magnetic or electric field, and hands every joule back in the next part.

And yet, for the purposes of calculating how much current flows, reactance behaves exactly like resistance. It has the same dimensions and the same unit, the ohm. So you can divide a voltage by a reactance and get a current, just as you would with R. Store versus dissipate is a question about energy, not about how big the current is.

Let us make the frequency dependence intuitive rather than memorised. An inductor opposes changes in current. Raise the frequency and you are demanding that the current reverse direction more and more violently, more times per second. So the inductor digs in harder, and its opposition grows. Hence X L rising with omega.

A capacitor is the mirror image. Rapid back-and-forth is exactly what it enjoys, because the charge never has time to build up and block anything. Slow the drive down and the capacitor gets time to charge fully, at which point it stops the current dead. So its opposition falls as frequency rises.

Push both of those to the D C limit, where frequency is zero, and you get the two facts examiners love as one-liners. X L equals omega L becomes zero, so an ideal inductor is a plain short circuit to D C. X C equals one over omega C blows up to infinity, so a capacitor is an open circuit and blocks D C completely.

<excited> And now look back at that graph one more time, because it contains a promise. Two opposite trends, one rising and one falling, must cross somewhere. At that crossing the two oppositions are equal and, as we will see, they cancel each other out entirely. That single point is resonance, and this chapter has been building towards it since the first line.
उस frequency-dependent विरोध को एक ठीक नाम चाहिए, और है। इसे reactance कहते हैं, capital X से लिखा जाता है, और यही inductor या capacitor resistance की जगह पेश करता है।

दोनों reactances लिखने में बेहद सरल और व्यवहार में बिल्कुल उल्टी हैं। Inductive reactance X L equals omega L, तो ये frequency के सीधे अनुपात में बढ़ती है। Capacitive reactance X C equals one over omega C, तो frequency बढ़ने पर ये गिरती है। एक चढ़ती है, एक ढहती है।

Graph विरोध को साफ़ कर देता है। नीली सीधी line X L है, origin से लगातार ऊपर जाती हुई। लाल curve X C है, कम frequency पर विशाल और फिर गिरती हुई। चूँकि एक चढ़ती है और दूसरी गिरती है, वो ठीक एक frequency पर मिलेंगी ही, जो हरे रंग में निशान है। वो crossing point याद रखिए; दो subtopic बाद यही पूरी resonance की कहानी होगी।

अब एक सचमुच अहम फ़र्क़। Reactance कोई अलग टोपी पहने हुए resistance नहीं है। Resistor बिजली की energy लेकर उसे अपरिवर्तनीय रूप से heat बना देता है। Reactance कुछ भी dissipate नहीं करती। वो cycle के एक हिस्से में energy लेती है, उसे magnetic या electric field में जमा करती है, और अगले हिस्से में हर joule लौटा देती है।

फिर भी, कितना current बहेगा ये गिनने के लिए reactance बिल्कुल resistance जैसी बर्ताव करती है। उसके वही dimensions हैं और वही unit, ohm। तो आप voltage को reactance से भाग देकर current निकाल सकते हैं, ठीक जैसे R के साथ करते। Store बनाम dissipate energy का सवाल है, current कितना बड़ा है इसका नहीं।

Frequency dependence को रटने की जगह intuitive बना लेते हैं। Inductor current के बदलाव का विरोध करता है। Frequency बढ़ाइए और आप माँग रहे हैं कि current और ज़्यादा हिंसक ढंग से, हर second और ज़्यादा बार, direction बदले। तो inductor और मज़बूती से अड़ जाता है, और उसका विरोध बढ़ता है। इसीलिए X L, omega के साथ चढ़ती है।

Capacitor इसका आईना है। तेज़ आगे-पीछे उसे यही पसंद है, क्योंकि charge को जमा होकर कुछ रोकने का समय ही नहीं मिलता। Drive धीमा कीजिए और capacitor को पूरा charge होने का समय मिल जाता है, और उसी पल वो current को रोक देता है। तो frequency बढ़ने पर उसका विरोध गिरता है।

दोनों को D C limit तक ले जाइए, जहाँ frequency zero है, और वो दो तथ्य मिलते हैं जिन्हें examiners one-liner बनाकर पूछते हैं। X L equals omega L बनकर zero हो जाता है, तो ideal inductor D C के लिए सादा short circuit है। X C equals one over omega C बढ़कर infinity हो जाता है, तो capacitor open circuit है और D C को पूरी तरह रोक देता है।

<excited> और अब उस graph को एक बार फिर देखिए, क्योंकि उसमें एक वादा छिपा है। दो उल्टी trends, एक चढ़ती और एक गिरती, कहीं न कहीं मिलेंगी ही। उस मिलन पर दोनों विरोध बराबर होते हैं और, जैसा हम देखेंगे, एक-दूसरे को पूरी तरह काट देते हैं। वही एक बिंदु resonance है, और ये chapter पहली line से उसी की तरफ़ बढ़ रहा है।
